hyperedges.label: The three rules
The machinery that refuses to invent a number
The machinery that keeps the board up
The absent-is-not-zero distinctions
Deriving the hub schedule
The spec sheet's absence discipline
The Settings panel's non-blocking contract
Rule 2 written into the markup itself
The three rules restated across every surface
One drawing rasterised at four sizes

nodes.label: Catalyst Console
nodes.rationale: A driver station companion for FRC teams running FrcCatalyst. Tauri app: small Rust backend, plain HTML/CSS/JS frontend in the Windows WebView2. No framework, no bundler, no runtime network fetch; installer under four megabytes.

nodes.label: Rule 1 — It never controls the robot
nodes.rationale: FRC requires the official NI Driver Station and only one DS may hold the robot connection. The console does not open that socket and has no code path that could. Enable, disable and E-stop belong exclusively to the Driver Station.
nodes.norm_label: rule 1 — it never controls the robot

nodes.label: Rule 2 — Nothing it does may impede driving
nodes.rationale: No modal blocks the dashboard, no check gates anything, no acknowledgement is ever required. Every failure degrades to a dimmed number and a quiet chip in the corner, so if the console breaks mid-match the driver keeps driving and need not notice.
nodes.norm_label: rule 2 — nothing it does may impede driving

nodes.label: Rule 3 — It never invents a number
nodes.rationale: A topic the robot has not published shows a dash, not a plausible value. The .dslog parser refuses versions it does not recognise rather than decoding them into nonsense. Demo data must be switched on deliberately and says so on screen while it runs.
nodes.norm_label: rule 3 — it never invents a number

nodes.label: NI Driver Station
nodes.rationale: The official FRC driver station. Only one may hold the robot connection, which is the whole basis of rule 1.

nodes.label: The second control path hazard
nodes.rationale: A tool that could drive would be a second control path to a robot, which is exactly what rule 1 forbids. Read-only is the design, not an unfinished feature.

nodes.label: The 10 Hz paint timer
nodes.rationale: The dashboard paints on a plain 10 Hz timer rather than only on requestAnimationFrame. Chromium stops firing animation frames for a window it considers occluded, so parking the Driver Station on top of an rAF-only dashboard would freeze it with stale numbers still on screen. This is rule 2 expressed as a repaint strategy.

nodes.label: Chromium stops rAF for an occluded window
nodes.rationale: The specific browser behaviour that makes an rAF-only dashboard unsafe on a driver station laptop, where the Driver Station window is routinely on top.
nodes.norm_label: chromium stops raf for an occluded window

nodes.label: One console at a time
nodes.rationale: Launching again hands off to the running process, raises it and exits. Two consoles would mean two NetworkTables clients on one robot and a driver reading whichever happened to be on top.

nodes.label: The /FMSInfo write guard
nodes.rationale: All of /FMSInfo is read-only from the console's side, enforced in nt_set at the backend boundary rather than in the UI, so the guard holds whatever the frontend asks for.

nodes.label: /FMSInfo topics
nodes.rationale: Control word, alliance colour, event and match number, and the game-specific message. Carries no match time at all.

nodes.label: /FMSInfo/GameSpecificMessage
nodes.rationale: Names which alliance's hub goes inactive first. The hub schedule is derived from it plus the alliance colour.

nodes.label: Match clock topic fallback chain
nodes.rationale: /FMSInfo carries no time, so robot code must publish one. The console tries /Catalyst/Match/TimeLeft, then /SmartDashboard/MatchTime, then /FMSInfo/MatchTime, and takes the first that exists. With none of them the match timer and hub countdown show dashes rather than counting down from a number nobody published — rule 3 applied to the clock.

nodes.label: Hub activation tile
nodes.rationale: Answers one question from across the drive station: is our hub active, and how long until that changes. Colour carries it, countdown large underneath.

nodes.label: HUB versus TOWER terminology
nodes.rationale: The HUB is the fuel goal and the thing that goes active and inactive; the TOWER is the climbing structure in the alliance wall with its three rungs. Getting it backwards on a competition dashboard is not a harmless nickname.

nodes.label: REBUILT teleop shift schedule
nodes.rationale: Teleop runs 140 s in six segments (2026 Game Manual, Table 6-2). Transition shift and end game have both hubs active by rule; shifts 1-4 alternate, with the alliance that scored more fuel in auto inactive first.

nodes.label: Waiting for FMS game data rather than guessing
nodes.rationale: Before the game-specific message arrives the tile says so rather than guessing, because during shifts the answer genuinely depends on an auto result nothing else can infer. Rule 3 applied to the hub schedule.
nodes.norm_label: waiting for fms game data rather than guessing

nodes.label: A robot-published answer always wins
nodes.rationale: If the robot would rather compute the hub schedule itself, publish a boolean and a countdown and configure the tile to read them. The robot's own answer overrides the console's derivation.

nodes.label: The robot's spec sheet
nodes.rationale: A robot on FrcCatalyst 1.10+ publishes its own account of itself under /Catalyst/Robot/ — name, drivetrain geometry, mass, power, and the Catalyst features it runs. Drawn to scale from its own published figures.

nodes.label: RobotIdentity.declare
nodes.rationale: One line in RobotContainer is the whole adoption; everything else the library derives rather than accepting as input.

nodes.label: Absence rather than a dash on the spec sheet
nodes.rationale: A key the robot did not publish produces no row, and an empty group produces no group. A dash on a Gyro row would say this robot has no gyro; absence says it did not mention one, and only the second is true. The one place the console inverts its own dash convention, and still rule 3.
nodes.norm_label: absence rather than a dash on the spec sheet

nodes.label: The Catalyst feature inventory
nodes.rationale: From 1.11 the sheet leads with which parts of the library the robot actually runs — Autopilot, Strategist, Sequence, Goal Director, Physics Core — each recorded by the component as it is built rather than declared anywhere. Two robots with the same drivetrain and motor count can still be completely different machines, and this is the only part of the sheet that says so.

nodes.label: Physics Core
nodes.rationale: Publishes pose, slip factor, tipping usage, traction usage and estimator confidence on its own once constructed. Slip, tipping and traction are all fraction-of-limit-in-use, so all three read the same way round: higher is worse.

nodes.label: Physics Core is advisory only
nodes.rationale: Physics Core has been validated in simulation and has never run on carpet; nothing on this dashboard should be gating a driver decision yet. The tile says advisory only on its face, deliberately.

nodes.label: The collision group and the Impacts tile
nodes.rationale: A new timestamp is what marks a new hit, rather than the same one still being reported.
nodes.norm_label: the collision group and the impacts tile

nodes.label: The tunables manifest
nodes.rationale: The robot declares in one JSON string at /Catalyst/Tunables/.manifest what it is willing to let a dashboard change. The console shows what is in that list and nothing else — it never infers that a topic looks tunable, so a value you did not declare cannot be changed from here.

nodes.label: Demo data
nodes.rationale: Synthetic telemetry for a board with no robot. Exists, has to be switched on deliberately, and says so on screen while it runs — the concession rule 3 makes, fenced so it cannot be mistaken for a robot.

nodes.label: Driver Station logs
nodes.rationale: The .dsevents and .dslog files the NI DS already writes, parsed into a timeline. Some of that exists nowhere else: the robot never sees its own packet loss, because the packets that would have told it are the ones that went missing.

nodes.label: The .dslog parser fails closed
nodes.rationale: The formats are community-reverse-engineered rather than documented by NI, so a header the parser does not recognise is reported as unparsed and the event log is still shown. Inventing a battery voltage would be worse than admitting the file cannot be read.

nodes.label: The read-only diagnostics MCP server
nodes.rationale: The same binary run with --mcp opens no window and serves read-only diagnostics over stdio so an agent can see what the robot is doing. Read-only is the whole design: a tool that could drive would be a second control path.

nodes.label: Two modes, one binary
nodes.rationale: catalyst-console launches a dashboard window; catalyst-console --mcp serves diagnostics on stdio instead. --help explains both.

nodes.label: Strict CSP and vendored three.js
nodes.rationale: npm run vendor copies three.js into src/vendor/ and must run before the first build: the webview runs under script-src 'self', so nothing loads from a CDN. A dashboard that needs the internet to draw a field is a dashboard that fails in exactly the venue it is meant for.

nodes.label: The baked field model
nodes.rationale: The KOP CAD glTF is 223 MB and 6.8 million vertices — a fine marketing asset and a terrible dashboard one. npm run field-cad decimates it to about 190k vertices and 6 MB, a 36x reduction that still reads as the REBUILT field. Deliberately not committed: it is FIRST's model rather than ours.

nodes.label: The procedural field outline
nodes.rationale: With no baked model the view draws the field from its dimensions — carpet, perimeter, driver station glass, centre and alliance lines. Not a placeholder to apologise for: it is what renders on a machine that has never seen the CAD, and it is the version that always works.

nodes.label: Field material re-grounding
nodes.rationale: The KOP model is lit for a render, so its unpainted parts arrive near-white — a slab of glare in a dark cockpit that pulls your eye away from the robot. Each material keeps its hue so alliance red and blue still read, but saturation and lightness come right down and the field recedes behind the thing you are actually watching.

nodes.label: Field render cost control
nodes.rationale: Because this shares a laptop with the Driver Station: 30 fps, no shadows, no textures, no post-processing, ~30 meshes, rendering stops entirely when the dashboard tab is not showing, and three.js is only fetched when a field tile exists in the layout.

nodes.label: 20 Hz batched flush
nodes.rationale: nt4.rs batches values into a map and flushes on a fixed cadence rather than emitting at wire rate. The robot publishes at 50 Hz across hundreds of topics; pushing each change straight into the webview would spend the whole frame budget in IPC. UI cost is made independent of how chatty the robot is.

nodes.label: Layout export and import
nodes.rationale: Export the board as JSON and every laptop in the pit comes up the same.

nodes.label: A stored board that cannot be read does not take the console with it
nodes.rationale: Each tile is checked on the way out of storage and an unreadable one is dropped with a console warning — silence and nine of ten tiles beats a dialog and none. If building the board throws anyway the console falls back to its shipped layout. Not tidiness: the build runs at module scope, so a throw there used to abort the rest of the file, taking the repaint loop, the keyboard listener and the panel stand-down with it and leaving a driver an empty board that still looked healthy. Storage is left untouched, because the board that could not be built is still the board somebody arranged.
nodes.norm_label: a stored board that cannot be read does not take the console with it

nodes.label: Candidate address cycling
nodes.rationale: The console cycles 127.0.0.1, roborio-TEAM-frc.local, 10.TE.AM.2 and 172.22.11.2 until one answers, so the same build works everywhere with no setting to forget.

nodes.label: The team number lives in the backend config
nodes.rationale: Kept by the backend in the app's own config directory rather than in the webview's storage, because --mcp has to read the same answer with no webview involved.
nodes.norm_label: the team number lives in the backend config

nodes.label: The Settings panel
nodes.rationale: One panel holding everything the console lets you change about itself, replacing a set of modals hanging off chips in the top strip, and About with them. A mode of the instrument rather than a window over it.

nodes.label: Settings stands down when the robot goes live
nodes.rationale: Nothing in the panel is modal, nothing has an apply button, and the whole panel stands down the instant the robot is enabled or E-stopped. That last part is rule two: whatever the console has to say about itself, none of it is worth reading over the top of a state lamp.
nodes.norm_label: settings stands down when the robot goes live

nodes.label: Settings search leaves matches where they live
nodes.rationale: Typing filters every row in every section at once and leaves each match where it lives, so a setting found by searching is changed the same way as one found by navigating — it is the same row, with the handler it was built with.
nodes.norm_label: settings search leaves matches where they live

nodes.label: Units, metric or imperial
nodes.rationale: Changes how the spec sheet reads and nothing else; the robot always publishes SI and nothing on the wire moves. It exists because FRC writes its frame perimeter and height rules in inches, so a team checking legality is otherwise converting by hand at exactly the moment they cannot afford an arithmetic mistake.

nodes.label: Settings storage is validated key by key
nodes.rationale: A value out of range is pulled back into it and anything else falls back to the default, because a bad number out of storage lands in a component that has no business validating a setting.
nodes.norm_label: settings storage is validated key by key

nodes.label: Competition legality
nodes.rationale: It is a dashboard: it connects to NetworkTables and displays what it finds, as Shuffleboard, Glass, Elastic and AdvantageScope all do. It does not touch the DS protocol and does not open a second control connection. The team is responsible for checking the season manual.

nodes.label: FrcCatalyst
nodes.rationale: The robot-side library this console is a companion to. Versions 1.10+ publish the spec sheet, 1.11+ the feature inventory, 1.12+ the CAN device tree.

nodes.label: Alert group topics
nodes.rationale: Catalyst's AlertManager publishes string arrays at /Catalyst/Alerts/Errors, Warnings and Info; WPILib's own widget uses lowercase errors/warnings/infos. The tile reads whichever is present rather than making you pick, and the group path is configurable.

nodes.label: Auto chooser
nodes.rationale: Standard SendableChooser. The console reads options and selected under the chooser path and writes selected when you pick one — the same key Shuffleboard writes. One of only two things the console ever writes.

nodes.label: Shortest distinguishing path suffix
nodes.rationale: With several topics on one gauge, labels are derived from the shortest path suffix that actually distinguishes them — four keys ending in /Velocity come out as FrontLeft / FrontRight / BackLeft / BackRight rather than Velocity four times.

nodes.label: Trust the robot, not the dashboard
nodes.rationale: If something here disagrees with what your robot is actually doing, trust the robot — because a dashboard that is confidently wrong is worse than one that says it does not know. The three rules stated as a disposition rather than a mechanism.
nodes.norm_label: trust the robot, not the dashboard

nodes.label: Documentation index
nodes.rationale: The docs landing page: installing, settings, the garage, widgets, the hub schedule, the diagnostics MCP server, and the contract with the robot.

nodes.label: The three rules, restated in the docs index
nodes.rationale: A compressed restatement of the same three rules the README states in full, placed at the head of the documentation set so every page is read under them.
nodes.norm_label: the three rules, restated in the docs index

nodes.label: The hub schedule
nodes.rationale: In REBUILT your alliance HUB stops scoring for part of teleop. The console works out when from the rules and the FMS game data, so the robot does not have to tell it.

nodes.label: Six teleop segments, Table 6-2
nodes.rationale: Teleop runs 140 s in six segments. The clock counts down, so each segment is named by the time remaining when it ends: transition 2:20-2:10, shifts 1-4 at 25 s each, end game 0:30-0:00.

nodes.label: Alternating shifts 1-4
nodes.rationale: The alliance that scored more fuel in AUTO is inactive for shift 1, then they alternate. On a tie FMS picks one at random, so the game data always names an alliance.

nodes.label: Game data is empty until after auto
nodes.rationale: /FMSInfo/GameSpecificMessage is a single character, R or B, naming the alliance whose goal goes inactive first. It is empty until roughly three seconds after auto ends, once fuel scoring has been assessed. That is why the tile says waiting for FMS game data early in a match rather than guessing.
nodes.norm_label: game data is empty until after auto

nodes.label: Auto, transition and end game need no game data
nodes.rationale: Both hubs are active by rule in those segments, and the tile says so rather than reporting an unknown. The schedule is only genuinely underdetermined during shifts 1-4.
nodes.norm_label: auto, transition and end game need no game data

nodes.label: /FMSInfo carries no match clock
nodes.rationale: That table has the control word, the alliance, the event and the game-specific message but no time. Robot code has to publish it with CatalystLog.log("Match/TimeLeft", DriverStation.getMatchTime()). Without it the timer and the hub countdown show dashes rather than inventing a number.

nodes.label: Installing Catalyst Console
nodes.rationale: Three ways in, in the order most teams should pick: with the Catalyst desktop app, the standalone installer, or from source.

nodes.label: Bundled with the Catalyst desktop app
nodes.rationale: A Driver Console entry appears in the sidebar. The console is a separate binary with its own release cadence, so the app asks whether one is bundled rather than offering a button that reports not found when pressed.
nodes.norm_label: bundled with the catalyst desktop app

nodes.label: The standalone installer
nodes.rationale: About 3.5 MB, Start Menu entry and desktop shortcut. The usual case for the machine that actually runs matches.

nodes.label: Building from source
nodes.rationale: npm install, npm run vendor, npm run build. Needs Rust and the WebView2 runtime that ships with Windows 11.

nodes.label: The optional field bakes
nodes.rationale: npm run field-cad bakes the KOP field CAD down to something a dashboard can carry; npm run field-collision derives collision geometry from it. Both optional — without them the field view draws itself from published dimensions.

nodes.label: The quiet update check
nodes.rationale: The console looks once at launch, quietly. If there is one a chip appears in the dock; if the machine cannot reach GitHub — on a field network the normal case — nothing appears at all. No prompt, no dialog, no interruption anywhere in this path, because an update notice is exactly the sort of thing rule two exists to keep away from a driver.

nodes.label: Signed releases
nodes.rationale: Releases are signed and the installer verifies the signature, so an update tampered with in transit is refused rather than run.

nodes.label: The diagnostics MCP server
nodes.rationale: Started with --mcp it opens no window: it connects to NetworkTables exactly as the dashboard does and speaks the Model Context Protocol on stdin and stdout, so an agent can ask what the robot is publishing.

nodes.label: There is no drive tool, and there will not be one
nodes.rationale: Every tool reads, none writes. No enable, no drive, no estop, and no nt_set either. The dashboard's own NetworkTables write path exists for tunables and auto choosers, is guarded against /FMSInfo, and is deliberately not reachable from mcp.rs. That is the first of the three rules holding, not a feature nobody got round to.
nodes.norm_label: there is no drive tool, and there will not be one

nodes.label: Diagnosis has never needed control
nodes.rationale: What the server is for is the other half of the problem: an agent that can see the robot's state can diagnose it. The argument that lets rule 1 and a useful agent surface coexist.

nodes.label: The nine read-only tools
nodes.rationale: console_status, nt_list, nt_get, alerts, physics, match_state, ds_sessions, ds_events, field_map. Start with console_status: every other tool reads more usefully once you know whether there is a robot on the other end.

nodes.label: Absent is not zero
nodes.rationale: The third rule applies here more than anywhere, because an agent cannot see the dash a driver would. A tile that shows an em dash is obviously empty; a tool that returns 0.0 is confidently wrong, and an agent will act on it. So every value carries whether it was actually published.

nodes.label: alerts returns null, not an empty list
nodes.rationale: An empty list reads as all clear, which is the most dangerous wrong answer this server could give. A missing group means the question was not answered, not that the robot is healthy.
nodes.norm_label: alerts returns null, not an empty list

nodes.label: match_state.mode is null without a control word
nodes.rationale: Not "Disabled". A robot nobody is hearing from is not a robot that is disabled.
nodes.norm_label: match_state.mode is null without a control word

nodes.label: Published-and-empty is not absent
nodes.rationale: FMS sends the game-specific message at the start of teleop, and the hub schedule depends on telling an empty published string apart from an absent topic.

nodes.label: console_status.rtt_ms is null while disconnected
nodes.rationale: A round trip measured on a link that has since dropped is a stale number, not a current one.

nodes.label: NaN comes back as the string "NaN"
nodes.rationale: JSON has no NaN and serialisers turn it into null — which in this server means not published. An uninitialised estimator publishes NaN often enough that conflating the two would be a real misreading. The type is still reported as double.
nodes.norm_label: nan comes back as the string "nan"

nodes.label: A quiet session is not an unreadable file
nodes.rationale: The .dslog formats are community-reverse-engineered rather than documented by NI, so a header the parser does not recognise is reported as unparsed rather than decoded into plausible nonsense.
nodes.norm_label: a quiet session is not an unreadable file

nodes.label: field_map says which paths it searched
nodes.rationale: The map is generated by npm run field-collision and is deliberately not committed, so a fresh checkout and an installed build both legitimately lack one. Saying where it looked turns an absence into an answer.
nodes.norm_label: field_map says which paths it searched

nodes.label: The advisory travels with the numbers
nodes.rationale: The Physics Core tile says advisory only on its face for a driver; an agent reading the same values deserves the same warning, and unlike a driver it cannot see the tile.
nodes.norm_label: the advisory travels with the numbers

nodes.label: Implemented without an MCP SDK
nodes.rationale: The surface a server this small needs is a few hundred lines, and a dependency for it would be more code to audit than the code it replaces, in a binary that ships to a driver station laptop.

nodes.label: stdout carries protocol frames and nothing else
nodes.rationale: Anything else on stdout corrupts the stream. Diagnostics for humans, and the NetworkTables client's own logging, go to stderr.
nodes.norm_label: stdout carries protocol frames and nothing else

nodes.label: JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio
nodes.rationale: One JSON object per line: initialize, tools/list, tools/call and ping. Protocol revisions 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26 and 2025-06-18 are all answered.

nodes.label: Two NetworkTables clients are ordinary
nodes.rationale: Running the server alongside the dashboard is fine — Shuffleboard and Glass coexist the same way. What must not be duplicated is the Driver Station, and neither of them is one. The distinction that makes rule 1 about control rather than about connections.

nodes.label: Failure, quietly and without lying
nodes.rationale: No robot is the normal state for most of a day and is not an error — the tools answer with connected:false and report the absence of each value rather than failing the call. The NetworkTables client reconnects on its own forever.

nodes.label: The garage
nodes.rationale: Settings to Robot shows the robot's own account of itself: its name, a plan drawn to scale, and the specification it published. Nothing on it is typed in and nothing is configurable — it fills in on its own the moment a robot that publishes a sheet connects, and stays blank when one does not.

nodes.label: One line of adoption
nodes.rationale: RobotIdentity.declare("Ratchet") at the top of RobotContainer is the whole adoption. FrcCatalyst 1.10+ derives the team number, season, roboRIO serial and image, library and WPILib versions, brownout threshold, CAN inventory, gyro, and — once a SwerveSubsystem exists — drivetrain type, module count and positions, track width, wheelbase, odometry rate and top speed.

nodes.label: Derived rather than passed in
nodes.rationale: None of it is passed in, and that is the point. Anything passed in can drift: a team that regears its drive and forgets to edit an identity block publishes last month's robot with this month's confidence.

nodes.label: A builder for the facts no API can answer
nodes.rationale: A tape measure is the only source for a frame perimeter, and only your own build knows which commit the robot code came from. Everything in the builder is optional; leaving one out costs you that row and nothing else.
nodes.norm_label: a builder for the facts no api can answer

nodes.label: Gear ratios and mass are the exceptions
nodes.rationale: Gear ratios come only from the module constants handed to .swerveModules(...), because Phoenix builds a SwerveDrivetrain from them and will not hand them back. Mass and moment of inertia come from the deployed PathPlanner settings; a project without them publishes neither.
nodes.norm_label: gear ratios and mass are the exceptions

nodes.label: Nothing has to be republished
nodes.rationale: NT4 keeps the last value of every topic and hands it to whoever subscribes next, so a console that connects mid-match, or reconnects after the radio drops, gets the sheet on connect. The library rewrites it when a new source of facts turns up, so declaration order does not matter.

nodes.label: The nine spec sheet groups
nodes.rationale: Catalyst, Software, Controller, Drivetrain, Chassis, Traction, Power, Hardware, Power channels — the plan first, then the name with team, season and controller model, then the sheet grouped the way a spec sheet is read.

nodes.label: Bumper diagonal and channels used
nodes.rationale: Two rows are worked out here rather than read: the bumper diagonal, which is the width that has to clear a gap on the angle, and channels used, which counts the named channels against the module's total. Both are arithmetic on published figures, and both disappear when either side they are built from does.

nodes.label: A count and a list answer different questions
nodes.rationale: The count answers how loaded is the PDH; the list answers which breaker is the one that just popped, and only the robot knows that. The same reasoning splits the CAN tree out into its own Devices section: a count is the right shape for a glance and a tree is the right shape for a diagnosis.
nodes.norm_label: a count and a list answer different questions

nodes.label: The Catalyst group leads the sheet
nodes.rationale: It leads because it is the part that distinguishes robots. Two machines can have identical drivetrains and motor counts and be nothing alike, because one scores on its own and the other does not. Nothing in the group is declared — each entry is written by the component at the moment it is constructed. A list maintained by hand is a list of what a team meant to use; this is a list of what came up.
nodes.norm_label: the catalyst group leads the sheet

nodes.label: Why a missing fact is missing rather than dashed
nodes.rationale: Everywhere else an unpublished value shows a dash because the tile is a fixed shape. The sheet is the one place that rule points the other way. A dash on a Gyro row says this robot has no gyro; absence says it did not mention one, and only the second is ever true — the console cannot tell a robot without a gyro from a robot on an older library, or one whose sheet was written before the gyro was constructed.
nodes.norm_label: why a missing fact is missing rather than dashed

nodes.label: The library omits rather than zeroes
nodes.rationale: A fact the library does not know is absent from the wire, not zero, not -1, not an empty string. Once a placeholder leaves the robot it is indistinguishable from a measurement. Rule 3 pushed back across the wire onto the robot side.
nodes.norm_label: the library omits rather than zeroes

nodes.label: The plan, drawn from the wire
nodes.rationale: The bumper outline, the frame inside it, and a wheel at each published module position sized off the published wheel radius. Nose points up, which is +x in WPILib's frame. Drawn from measurements rather than picked from stock pictures because wrong dimensions look wrong: a team that published a 30-inch frame should see a 30-inch frame.
nodes.norm_label: the plan, drawn from the wire

nodes.label: Partial figures give a partial drawing
nodes.rationale: With no bumper figures the outer edge is dashed; with no frame figures the deck is left out; with module positions alone the wheels sit inside a dashed outline taken from their own span; with none of the three there is no plan at all. The caption says what it was built from, so nobody reads one for the other.
nodes.norm_label: partial figures give a partial drawing

nodes.label: The plan is not painted in the alliance colour
nodes.rationale: Alone among everything else on this dashboard that has bumpers. Alliance is match state: it flips between matches and a team carries both sets. A spec sheet that changed colour depending on when you opened it would be describing the match rather than the machine, and the machine is the same robot on either side.
nodes.norm_label: the plan is not painted in the alliance colour

nodes.label: Copy the spec sheet
nodes.rationale: Writes the whole thing to the clipboard as plain text in the selected units. At inspection someone is reading frame perimeter and weight off a screen and writing them onto a form; this is that without the transcription step. Written from the same data the panel rendered rather than derived a second time, so the text cannot disagree with the screen. If the clipboard refuses it says so rather than claiming a copy that did not happen.

nodes.label: The demo sheet is deliberately incomplete
nodes.rationale: No camera list, no drive ratio — because that is the ordinary case, and the panel leaving those lines out is the behaviour worth demonstrating. Named Demo robot so nobody mistakes it for their own.
nodes.norm_label: the demo sheet is deliberately incomplete

nodes.label: The Settings panel, section by section
nodes.rationale: Everything the console lets you change about itself, in one panel. It replaced the modals that used to hang off the chips in the top strip and the About page with them. Opened with the gear or S; the link chip goes to Robot with the team field focused, L to Dashboard, and the wordmark, ? and F1 to About.
nodes.norm_label: the settings panel, section by section

nodes.label: Nothing applies
nodes.rationale: There is no apply button and no confirmation step, because a control is the truth the moment you move it. The surface that changed a setting is responsible for making the board agree with it, and does so immediately.

nodes.label: Nothing is modal
nodes.rationale: No focus trap, no inert dashboard behind it, and the markup does not claim otherwise. It is a mode you step out of rather than a window that holds you — claiming modality would have been the markup saying one thing while the program did another.

nodes.label: It stands down
nodes.rationale: The moment the robot is enabled or E-stopped the panel closes itself along with anything else covering the board. Rule two: a driver who opened Settings in the pit and then got called to the field must not find the state lamp, the match timer and the E-stop indicator behind a panel.

nodes.label: Searching leaves matches where they live
nodes.rationale: Nothing is cloned into a results list — the row you find is the row itself, with the handler it was built with. The label, its explanation and any text on the control are all searched, so 'inches' finds Units, whose own word is 'Imperial'. A query that matches nothing says so, quoting what you typed. Escape clears the filter; a second Escape closes the panel. About holds prose rather than rows, so it never matches and never claims to.
nodes.norm_label: searching leaves matches where they live

nodes.label: The Devices section
nodes.rationale: The sheet answers what is this robot; this answers what is on it and where, which is a different question asked at a different time. CAN devices as a tree, one group per bus, needing FrcCatalyst 1.12+ which publishes Hardware/Devices as bus|id|type. Neither half is a setting, so neither is reachable by search.

nodes.label: The power board is drawn only from a published channel count
nodes.rationale: It appears only when the robot published a channel count — a strip sized to whatever happens to be in use would be inventing the shape of a distribution board nobody described. Rule 3 applied to a drawing rather than to a number.
nodes.norm_label: the power board is drawn only from a published channel count

nodes.label: Trail length applies on release
nodes.rationale: Applied on release rather than during the drag, because the trail buffer is allocated when the scene is built, so changing the length is a rebuild.

nodes.label: One camera, two surfaces, one function
nodes.rationale: The buttons in the tile's own corner move the same setting as the Settings row; there is one camera and both surfaces go through one function to change it, because a tile quietly holding a camera of its own is how the two came to disagree.
nodes.norm_label: one camera, two surfaces, one function

nodes.label: Opens on applies at launch only
nodes.rationale: Setting it does not switch the view now, because that would be the setting acting on the wrong occasion.
nodes.norm_label: opens on applies at launch only

nodes.label: An import is checked whole before anything is applied
nodes.rationale: A document with one bad tile is refused with the reason, and the board on screen is left alone. A half-applied layout would be worse than a refused one.
nodes.norm_label: an import is checked whole before anything is applied

nodes.label: Reset arms itself rather than opening a dialog
nodes.rationale: Two presses rather than a dialog — the button arms itself and disarms after four seconds — because rule two says nothing blocks the board.
nodes.norm_label: reset arms itself rather than opening a dialog

nodes.label: Alert hold
nodes.rationale: How long a cleared alert stays on screen, dimmed, 0 to 8 s. Applied live on the drag since nothing has to be rebuilt. Robot alerts sitting near their threshold raise and clear repeatedly, and a tile that strobes next to a driver is worse than useless.

nodes.label: Demo data is amber, alone among the switches
nodes.rationale: Off by default and never remembered, the dock button stays lit the whole time it runs, and switching it on stands this panel down exactly as a robot enabling does. A dashboard that quietly invents telemetry is a hazard, so every part of that is deliberate. The duplicate switch in the dock is on purpose: while demo runs the fact that the numbers are invented has to be visible on the dashboard itself.
nodes.norm_label: demo data is amber, alone among the switches

nodes.label: Release notes are shown as plain text, never rendered
nodes.rationale: The notes are shown before you decide rather than after — the page is a decision rather than a changelog. The text arrived over the network, so it is shown as plain text and never rendered as markup.
nodes.norm_label: release notes are shown as plain text, never rendered

nodes.label: About lays the three rules across on a wide window
nodes.rationale: On a window 1080px or wider the three rules sit side by side rather than stacked, so they are read across rather than scrolled through: they are one idea in three parts, and a reader who has to scroll to reach the third has stopped holding the first two. Narrower than that it folds back to one column.
nodes.norm_label: about lays the three rules across on a wide window

nodes.label: Frames counts real NetworkTables frames only
nodes.rationale: Demo ticks are not NetworkTables frames, and counting them would be the console inventing a number about itself. Rule 3 turned inward on the console's own diagnostics.
nodes.norm_label: frames counts real networktables frames only

nodes.label: Bundled but switched off says exactly that
nodes.rationale: A model that is bundled but switched off reports itself as such, rather than reporting a preference as a fact about the build.
nodes.norm_label: bundled but switched off says exactly that

nodes.label: Every binding is a single unmodified key
nodes.rationale: A driver station is operated under pressure and often without looking down. That is exactly why typing in any field suspends them all: a bare d must never toggle demo data while somebody is halfway through typing a topic path. Escape in a field means abandon what I am typing and blurs it; a second Escape closes what is open.
nodes.norm_label: every binding is a single unmodified key

nodes.label: Storage is read one key at a time and every key is checked
nodes.rationale: A number outside its range is pulled back into it and anything else falls back to the default, because storage can hold anything — an older build wrote it, someone edited it by hand, a quota error truncated it — and a bad value out of there lands in a component that has no business validating a setting. Everything lives in local storage except the team number, which belongs to the backend because the MCP server has to read it with no webview involved.
nodes.norm_label: storage is read one key at a time and every key is checked

nodes.label: The widget catalogue
nodes.rationale: Every tile binds to NetworkTables keys you choose, so none of it is hard-coded to a season or a robot. Grouped as Match, Telemetry, Health, Field and Pit.

nodes.label: The component registry
nodes.rationale: The registry in src/app.js takes a config schema, a render that builds DOM once, and an update called each frame.

nodes.label: update must be cheap and must not throw
nodes.rationale: One bad tile cannot be allowed to take out the board, and the paint loop enforces that. The registry contract as an expression of rule 2.
nodes.norm_label: update must be cheap and must not throw

nodes.label: Alerts are held after they clear
nodes.rationale: Held for a couple of seconds after they clear, dimmed. Anything edge-triggered on a measurement sitting near its threshold raises and clears repeatedly, and rendering that verbatim gives a tile that strobes next to a driver.
nodes.norm_label: alerts are held after they clear

nodes.label: The chase camera swings around occluding field elements
nodes.rationale: Rather than leaving you looking at the back of a truss.
nodes.norm_label: the chase camera swings around occluding field elements

nodes.label: The app shell
nodes.rationale: One root div carrying the whole live state as data attributes — data-live, data-edit, data-linked, data-estop — with the top strip, the four views, and the dock inside it. The CSS reads the state off the root rather than each surface tracking it.

nodes.label: The top strip
nodes.rationale: The wordmark, the link chip, Driver Station and FMS lamps, the loop time, the view tablist and the gear. The wordmark opens Settings on About — a discreet target rather than a dock button, because the board and the dock are working surfaces and neither has room for vanity.

nodes.label: The tablist is one tab stop with arrow keys inside it
nodes.rationale: Not four tab stops in a row. The roving tabindex is maintained by showView; the arrows are wired by wireTablist.
nodes.norm_label: the tablist is one tab stop with arrow keys inside it

nodes.label: The four views
nodes.rationale: Dashboard, Tune, Logs and Topics as tabpanels; the board is a grid of tiles and the other three are sheets.

nodes.label: The dock
nodes.rationale: The state lamp with its name and source, edit layout, add component, the drop chip, the RTT chip and the demo button.

nodes.label: The drop chip appears only once the link has dropped
nodes.rationale: Silence is the normal state. A chip that is always there reporting zero is a chip a driver learns to stop reading.
nodes.norm_label: the drop chip appears only once the link has dropped

nodes.label: The demo switch is duplicated on purpose
nodes.rationale: Demo data is also a row in Settings, and that duplication is deliberate: while demo runs, the fact that the numbers are invented has to be visible on the dashboard itself, not filed away behind a panel nobody has open.
nodes.norm_label: the demo switch is duplicated on purpose

nodes.label: The Settings dialog deliberately carries no aria-modal
nodes.rationale: There is no focus trap and the dashboard behind is not inert, and that is the design rather than an oversight: rule two says nothing may impede driving, so this is a mode you step out of and not a window that holds you. Claiming modality would have been the markup saying one thing while the program did another.
nodes.norm_label: the settings dialog deliberately carries no aria-modal

nodes.label: The settings rail and its search box
nodes.rationale: Seven sections down the left — Robot, Devices, Field view, Dashboard, Data, Updates, About — with a search box above them. Typing filters every row in every section at once and leaves them where they are, so a match is changed in place rather than in a copy of itself.
nodes.norm_label: the settings rail and its search box

nodes.label: The garage card markup
nodes.rationale: A canvas for the plan, the name and sub-line, the spec groups, a copy button, and an empty state that says no robot has introduced itself. Nothing here is filled in by the console — a robot that publishes no sheet gets the empty state, and a group whose keys are absent does not appear at all.

nodes.label: Every control sharing the row's right edge sits in an .sctl
nodes.rationale: Including the ones wide enough to look like they hold that edge on their own — they agree at this width and diverge below 760px, where .sctl is what re-anchors them. Three controls are outside one and none of them wants to be in it: the address list and the paste box are the full width of a stacked row, and the hidden file input has no box to align. A wrapper that does nothing would be a worse lie than the note this replaced.
nodes.norm_label: every control sharing the row's right edge sits in an .sctl

nodes.label: What happened goes under the rows, not inside one
nodes.rationale: The same as the team note and the update note. A row says what a control does; what happened when you used it is the section speaking.
nodes.norm_label: what happened goes under the rows, not inside one

nodes.label: Paste it in by hand is the floor under import
nodes.rationale: Its own row rather than an appendage. On a laptop with no file dialog and no clipboard permission this is the only way in, and it is where an export lands when there is nowhere else to put it.
nodes.norm_label: paste it in by hand is the floor under import

nodes.label: The demo toggle is amber, alone among the switches
nodes.rationale: A .tog.hazard rather than the ordinary blue switch, because it is the one control on the panel that makes the console stop telling the truth about the robot.
nodes.norm_label: the demo toggle is amber, alone among the switches

nodes.label: Release notes render into a pre, never as markup
nodes.rationale: The text is the release's own, so it is shown as plain text rather than rendered: a note that arrived over the network is not markup this program should be executing.
nodes.norm_label: release notes render into a pre, never as markup

nodes.label: The three rules, as About renders them
nodes.rationale: An ordered list numbered 01, 02, 03 under the line 'Everything here answers to these, in order, and they are not negotiable.' The one place in the running program where the rules are stated to the user rather than merely obeyed.
nodes.norm_label: the three rules, as about renders them

nodes.label: The live diagnostics grid
nodes.rationale: Connected to, round trip, topics, running for, NT frames and link drops, plus whether this build bundles the field model and the collision map.

nodes.label: The import map points three at the vendored copy
nodes.rationale: three.js and its loaders import the bare specifier 'three'; the import map points it at ./vendor/three.module.min.js so nothing reaches for a CDN under the strict CSP.
nodes.norm_label: the import map points three at the vendored copy

nodes.label: The project banner
nodes.rationale: A 1200x320 hand-authored SVG banner on a near-black vertical gradient with a soft radial light pool at upper right. Left half: the red bolt mark at 2.55x scale, the wordmark 'Catalyst' in heavy white beside 'Console' in light grey, a one-line strapline, and a red-to-transparent sweep rule under it. Right half: a suggested dashboard. Not a photograph or a screenshot — the whole thing is drawn in primitives so it stays a few kilobytes and renders under the same no-network constraint the app itself works under.

nodes.label: The board, suggested rather than drawn
nodes.rationale: Six rounded dark rectangles at 50% opacity stand in for tiles, with one blue trace polyline, one green gauge arc on a grey track, and two progress bars — one red, one amber. Enough to read as instruments without being a legible screenshot: this is a dashboard of tiles, and that is the one thing a banner should say before any words do.
nodes.norm_label: the board, suggested rather than drawn

nodes.label: The three rules set in monospace on the banner
nodes.rationale: Three numbered monospace lines at the foot of the left column — 01 It never controls the robot, 02 Nothing it does may impede driving, 03 It never invents a number — set in a dim grey rather than the headline white. The source comment says why they are there at all: 'The three rules, because they are the product.' The rules appear in the marketing artwork, the README, the docs index and the running About panel, which is four independent restatements of the same three sentences.
nodes.norm_label: the three rules set in monospace on the banner

nodes.label: The console's own palette
nodes.rationale: Catalyst red #e94560 for the mark and the sweep, near-black grounds #16171b to #0a0b0d, grey #9a9ba1 for secondary text, with status colours quoted in the mock tiles: blue #4d90fe for a trace, green #30d158 for a healthy gauge, amber #ff9f0a for a warning bar. The source calls the ground 'The console's own ground, not the library's. Siblings rather than copies' — deliberately adjacent to FrcCatalyst's identity without being derived from it.

nodes.label: The application icon
nodes.rationale: A steering wheel drawn as a flat outline in Catalyst red on a near-black rounded square: an outer ring, a hub, one spoke to twelve o'clock and two falling to about four and eight. Squared-off shoulders on the lower spokes give it the silhouette of a racing wheel rather than a car's. No text, no bolt mark — the icon does not reuse the wordmark's lightning glyph.

nodes.label: The steering wheel motif
nodes.rationale: The mark says driver station rather than robot: a wheel is what the human holds, which is the half of the system this product serves. Read against rule 1 it is a deliberate near-miss — the app is named for the driver's seat and iconified with a control the app itself explicitly refuses to be.

nodes.label: The 32px application icon
nodes.rationale: The same steering wheel at taskbar and title-bar size. At 32px the hub and spokes fuse into a single mass and only the ring, the gaps and the red-on-black contrast survive, which is what makes it findable on a driver station taskbar next to the NI Driver Station.

nodes.label: The 128px application icon
nodes.rationale: The same artwork at desktop-shortcut size, where the three spokes and the hub separate cleanly.

nodes.label: The 128px @2x application icon
nodes.rationale: The 256px rendering of the same steering wheel for high-DPI displays. The set is one drawing rasterised at four sizes rather than four separately optimised marks.

nodes.label: The Tauri icon set
nodes.rationale: One steering-wheel drawing rasterised at 32, 128, 256 and full size for the Windows installer, the taskbar and the shortcut. Consistent with the banner's palette — the same Catalyst red on the same near-black — but not with its glyph, since the banner leads with the bolt and the icon with the wheel.
